title: ACID
description: Understand atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability through transaction failures, concurrent updates, storage-engine limits and safe retry reasoning.
notes:
## Give a transaction a precise reliability contract

ACID names four properties associated with reliable transactions: atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Together they help an application reason about changes despite failures and concurrent work. They do not guarantee that arbitrary application code is correct. A perfectly atomic transaction can commit an incorrect calculation, and a durable mistake remains a mistake until an authorized corrective action repairs it.

Imagine moving five reserved workshop seats from one allocation bucket to another. The intended operation subtracts five from the source and adds five to the destination without creating or losing capacity. Its contract includes permitted actors, nonnegative remaining capacity and one intended request identity. Transaction properties support that contract, while the application must still define and enforce its business meaning.

## Atomicity covers the chosen transaction boundary

Atomicity means the transaction's supported changes commit together or do not remain committed as a partial transaction. If the second seat update fails, the first should not be left as an independently committed subtraction. The guarantee only covers work inside the transaction on participating transactional resources. Two updates performed under separate autocommitted statements are two transactions, regardless of the function name surrounding them.

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE seat_buckets SET reserved = reserved - 5 WHERE bucket_id = 1;
UPDATE seat_buckets SET reserved = reserved + 5 WHERE bucket_id = 2;
-- The trusted workflow checks the required invariants before choosing:
ROLLBACK;
```

This illustration intentionally rolls back the changes. A successful SQL statement is not necessarily a successful business operation: an UPDATE matching zero rows may complete without a database error. Verify required row existence and affected-row meaning within the chosen workflow. Atomicity cannot detect that a missing destination was unacceptable unless the implementation actually checks that condition.

## Consistency preserves specified valid states

Consistency means a transaction should take the database from one valid state to another under the specified invariants. Database constraints can enforce required identities, valid references, uniqueness and particular row conditions. Application logic may need additional checks for rules involving several rows or external decisions. The engine does not invent those rules from a table's suggestive name.

For the seat transfer, a nonnegative source and unchanged combined capacity are separate requirements. Subtracting five from a source containing only three violates the intended rule even if both arithmetic statements execute. A transaction that instead credits the destination by six is atomic but changes the combined quantity. Write the invariant first, then identify which trusted mechanism enforces each part.

ACID consistency differs from the consistency terminology in the CAP theorem. CAP's consistency is generally modeled as linearizability: operations behave as if they occurred at one point between invocation and response. It is not merely every replica eventually having equal values. Keep state-validity rules and distributed observation guarantees distinct when using the same familiar word.

## Isolation governs interaction with concurrent work

Isolation describes which concurrent interactions an execution model permits and what observations transactions can make. Serializable execution provides a strong serial-equivalence model, but common SQL isolation levels permit different anomalies. Saying a database supports transactions does not prove that every report or read-modify-write sequence has the strongest isolation behavior.

Two requests can each read the same available capacity, both decide it is sufficient and then make incompatible decisions. Correct handling can require locking, a suitable atomic conditional update, constraints or serializable execution with retry, depending on the complete operation. Do not select a technique solely from an acronym. Trace the reads, predicates, writes and failure paths under the actual engine contract.

Isolation also does not mean every transaction physically runs alone. Independent operations can interleave while preserving the required observation model. Concurrency control may use locks, multiple row versions or combinations of techniques. The performance and blocking consequences depend on the workload, implementation and chosen level; serial-equivalent results do not require a literal one-transaction-at-a-time server.

## Durability begins with a successful commit contract

Durability concerns the survival of committed changes under the system's documented failure and persistence guarantees. Logging and recovery mechanisms help make that possible. A row becoming visible in one session before commit does not establish durability. Nor does printing a success message before the database confirms the intended transaction outcome.

Real guarantees depend on engine configuration and storage behavior. A relaxed persistence setting, failed storage subsystem or loss of an entire machine can exceed a local crash guarantee. Backups, replication and restore procedures address additional failure scopes. Avoid teaching durability as a promise that no imaginable disaster can ever lose data or that backups become unnecessary.

A client can also lose the connection while a commit response is in flight. The transaction may have committed even though the client did not receive confirmation. This is an unknown outcome, not automatic evidence of rollback. Reconciliation using an authorized request identity can distinguish an already completed operation from a new attempt without blindly repeating the business effect.

## Verify the storage engine and all participants

MySQL supports storage engines with different transactional capabilities. InnoDB supplies transactional facilities used by these examples. MyISAM does not provide equivalent rollback of its table changes. An application must inspect actual table definitions rather than assume that writing START TRANSACTION changes every storage engine into a transactional one.

Mixing transactional and nontransactional tables can leave effects that rollback cannot reverse. Likewise, ordinary DDL can have implicit commit behavior distinct from row updates. A transaction containing an email send, remote payment request or file write does not automatically make those external actions part of the database rollback domain. State exactly which participants share the atomic boundary.

## Handle errors without assuming their scope

Errors can affect a statement, a whole transaction or a connection depending on their cause and engine behavior. An InnoDB deadlock can roll back a transaction; other errors may roll back only the failed statement while earlier changes remain pending. The caller should inspect the documented failure semantics and explicitly close or discard an unsuccessful transaction rather than guess that any exception has undone everything.

Transaction cleanup belongs on every exit path. Returning a connection to a pool with an open transaction can leak locks or unexpected session state into later work. A failed rollback or lost connection also requires handling. Do not report a confirmed business failure or success merely because cleanup was attempted; distinguish confirmed rollback, confirmed commit and uncertain outcome.

## Keep retries and external actions coherent

Retrying the complete business operation can be appropriate after a retryable conflict, but use bounded attempts and a stable request identity. A duplicate-key conflict does not itself prove that the same authorized payload already succeeded. Verify ownership and meaning before interpreting it as an idempotent result. Unbounded retries can turn contention into persistent overload.

For external notifications, a reviewed transactional-outbox design can commit an event record with the database change and deliver it afterward. That separates database atomicity from network delivery while introducing its own idempotency and monitoring responsibilities. It is a design option rather than proof that every notification system is already reliable. Never claim one local transaction atomically controls unrelated services without an actual shared protocol.

## Test properties with targeted failure scenarios

For an atomicity exercise, begin with source capacity ten and destination capacity twenty. Subtract five, then simulate an application-detected invalid destination before commit. Predict the correct rollback result and explain why two autocommitted updates would fail that requirement. Add the case where the destination UPDATE matches no row but raises no error.

For an isolation exercise, write two sessions that both observe the same source capacity before either commits. Identify the business anomaly a naive stale-value assignment could permit. Then describe which trusted condition or serialization mechanism must prevent it. A one-session query returning the expected total cannot establish that concurrent execution is safe.

A durability exercise needs a documented crash and restart environment plus persistence settings; a normal SELECT after COMMIT is only a much narrower observation. Keep allowed, denied, failure and recovery evidence separate. Read [atomicity](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/atomicity), [isolation](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/isolation) and [durability](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/durability) for the individual properties. The useful outcome is an explicit transaction boundary and a tested account of what each failure leaves behind.

questions.question_text: What does the A in ACID stand for?
questions.explanation: Atomicity is the all-or-nothing guarantee.

questions.question_text: What does the D in ACID stand for?
questions.explanation: Committed changes survive failures within the documented persistence contract; engine settings and storage assumptions matter.

questions.question_text: Which listed MySQL storage engine lacks transactional rollback of its table changes?
questions.explanation: MyISAM is nontransactional. ROLLBACK cannot reverse its writes, and diagnostics can warn about incomplete rollback.

questions.question_text: Is ACID's 'Consistency' the same concept as the 'Consistency' in the CAP theorem?
options: No: ACID consistency concerns valid-state invariants, while CAP consistency is generally linearizability
CAP theorem doesn't have a Consistency concept
ACID Consistency only applies to distributed databases
questions.explanation: Linearizability describes observations appearing to occur at a single point between invocation and response, rather than merely eventual replica agreement.

questions.question_text: Why is choosing a transactional storage engine a prerequisite for ACID guarantees?
options: Multi-statement rollback requires transaction-capable participants; a nontransactional table is outside that guarantee
ACID guarantees are provided by the SQL language itself, independent of storage engine
Only Consistency requires a transactional engine
questions.explanation: ACID is only meaningful when the underlying engine actually implements transaction support.

questions.question_text: How do Atomicity and Consistency interact?
options: Atomicity partly enables Consistency — an incomplete (non-atomic) update could leave the database in an invalid, inconsistent state
questions.explanation: The four ACID properties aren't fully independent — atomicity helps guarantee consistency is achievable.

questions.question_text: What does the isolation contract specify for concurrent transactions?
options: It has no relationship to the other three
Which concurrent interactions and observations are allowed; weaker levels can permit anomalies
It only matters for single-user databases
It replaces the need for Atomicity entirely
questions.explanation: Isolation depends on the selected level and engine semantics, rather than a universal claim that all in-progress observations are forbidden.

questions.question_text: What is the overall purpose of the ACID guarantees together?
options: To make transactions a reliable building block for correct application logic despite concurrency, failures, and bugs
To reduce the amount of disk storage used
questions.explanation: ACID's combined purpose is trustworthiness of transactions under real-world conditions.

questions.question_text: Both updates autocommit separately. Does their shared function name make them atomic together?
options: No, the database boundaries remain separate
questions.explanation: The application must actually establish one participating transaction.

questions.question_text: The source subtraction succeeds and the destination UPDATE matches zero rows. What must the workflow do?
options: Check the required effect and choose rollback when the contract failed
questions.explanation: Statement completion does not prove the requested entity existed.

questions.question_text: A transaction subtracts5 and credits6. Which statement is correct?
options: It can be atomic while violating the capacity invariant
questions.explanation: Business consistency needs the correct calculation and enforcement.

questions.question_text: Does transactional support imply every query runs at SERIALIZABLE?
options: No, actual isolation settings and semantics matter
questions.explanation: Transaction capability and selected isolation level are distinct.

questions.question_text: A commit response is lost. What is the client outcome?
options: Permission to repeat without a request key
questions.explanation: The server may have committed before the response disappeared.

questions.question_text: Can a database rollback automatically unsend an email?
options: Only if email contains an ID
No, external effects need their own coordination
questions.explanation: The email server is outside the ordinary local transaction boundary.

questions.question_text: What is a useful purpose of a stable request identity?
options: Prove every duplicate error is success
Reconcile retries without blindly duplicating a business effect
questions.explanation: The stored result still needs an authorized payload match.

questions.question_text: Can a statement error leave earlier transaction changes pending?
options: Yes, depending on the engine and error scope
Only if there is no index
questions.explanation: Handle documented statement versus whole-transaction failure semantics.

questions.question_text: What does the C in CAP generally refer to?
questions.explanation: This differs from ACID state-validity consistency.

questions.question_text: What additional protection does a backup address?
options: Recovery scopes beyond the local commit guarantee
questions.explanation: Durability and disaster recovery need explicit failure models.

questions.question_text: Why is one successful transfer fixture insufficient isolation evidence?
options: It contains no competing session interleaving
questions.explanation: Concurrency properties require appropriate concurrent scenarios.

questions.question_text: What should be recorded with a transaction reliability claim?
questions.explanation: Claims must match the tested enforcement and recovery point.

coding_not_applicable: ACID properties require failure, concurrent-session and crash/restart verification at their actual enforcement points. The notes contain explicit failure-analysis exercises and transactional SQL. Deterministic single-result judging would not establish these guarantees.

CAP theorem doesn't have a Consistency concept
ACID Consistency only applies to distributed databases

original_questions.question_text: What role does Isolation play among the four ACID properties?
options: It has no relationship to the other three
It prevents concurrent transactions from seeing each other's not-yet-complete, in-progress state, which could otherwise violate atomicity's guarantees from an outside observer's perspective
It only matters for single-user databases
It replaces the need for Atomicity entirely
original_questions.explanation: Isolation protects the illusion of atomicity when multiple transactions run concurrently.

To reduce the amount of disk storage used
